source_block_templates.fs-id1165135194500: Gasoline costs have experienced some wild fluctuations over the last several decades. {{link:0}}{{child:0}} lists the average cost, in dollars, of a gallon of gasoline for the years 2005–2012. The cost of gasoline can be considered as a function of year.

Reading the rows as ordered pairs, we have: (2005, 2.31), (2006, 2.62), (2007, 2.84), (2008, 3.30), (2009, 2.41), (2010, 2.84), (2011, 3.58), and (2012, 3.68).
source_block_templates.fs-id1165133097252: If we were interested only in how the gasoline prices changed between 2005 and 2012, we could compute that the cost per gallon had increased from $2.31 to $3.68, an increase of $1.37. While this is interesting, it might be more useful to look at how much the price changed per year. In this section, we will investigate changes such as these.

If we use only the beginning and ending data, we would be finding the {{term:1}} over the specified period of time. source_block_templates.fs-id1165135440486/title: Using a Graph to Determine Where a Function is Increasing, Decreasing, or Constant
source_block_templates.fs-id1165137784644: As part of exploring how functions change, we can identify intervals over which the function is changing in specific ways. We say that a function is increasing on an interval if the function values increase as the input values increase within that interval. Similarly, a function is decreasing on an interval if the function values decrease as the input values increase over that interval. The average rate of change of an increasing function is positive, and the average rate of change of a decreasing function is negative. {{link:0}} shows examples of increasing and decreasing intervals on a function.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135390884/alt: Graph of a polynomial that shows the increasing and decreasing intervals and local maximum and minimum.
source_block_templates.Figure_01_03_004/caption: The function {{math:0}} is increasing on {{math:1}} and is decreasing on {{math:2}}
source_block_templates.fs-id1165134272749: While some functions are increasing (or decreasing) over their entire domain, many others are not. A value of the input where a function changes from increasing to decreasing (as we go from left to right, that is, as the input variable increases) is the location of a {{term:0}}. The function value at that point is the local maximum. If a function has more than one, we say it has local maxima. Similarly, a value of the input where a function changes from decreasing to increasing as the input variable increases is the location of a {{term:1}}. The function value at that point is the local minimum. The plural form is “local minima.” Together, local maxima and minima are called {{term:2}}, or local extreme values, of the function. (The singular form is “extremum.”) Often, the term local is replaced by the term relative. In this text, we will use the term local.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165134547216: Clearly, a function is neither increasing nor decreasing on an interval where it is constant. A function is also neither increasing nor decreasing at extrema. Note that we have to speak of local extrema, because any given local extremum as defined here is not necessarily the highest maximum or lowest minimum in the function’s entire domain.

The curve shows that the function is increasing from the left until it reaches a local maximum at the point (-2, 16), where it is noted that the local maximum is 16 and occurs at x = -2. Following this, the function decreases, passing through the origin, until it reaches a local minimum at the point (2, -16), with the caption indicating a local minimum of -16 occurring at x = 2. After this point, the function begins to increase again towards the right.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165133316450: To locate the local maxima and minima from a graph, we need to observe the graph to determine where the graph attains its highest and lowest points, respectively, within an open interval. Like the summit of a roller coaster, the graph of a function is higher at a local maximum than at nearby points on both sides. The graph will also be lower at a local minimum than at neighboring points. {{link:0}} illustrates these ideas for a local maximum.

source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/1: A rate of change relates a change in an output quantity to a change in an input quantity. The average rate of change is determined using only the beginning and ending data. See {{link:0}}.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/2: Identifying points that mark the interval on a graph can be used to find the average rate of change. See {{link:0}}.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/3: Comparing pairs of input and output values in a table can also be used to find the average rate of change. See {{link:0}}.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/4: An average rate of change can also be computed by determining the function values at the endpoints of an interval described by a formula. See {{link:0}} and {{link:1}}.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/5: The average rate of change can sometimes be determined as an expression. See {{link:0}}.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/6: A function is increasing where its rate of change is positive and decreasing where its rate of change is negative. See {{link:0}}.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/7: A local maximum is where a function changes from increasing to decreasing and has an output value larger (more positive or less negative) than output values at neighboring input values.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/8: A local minimum is where the function changes from decreasing to increasing (as the input increases) and has an output value smaller (more negative or less positive) than output values at neighboring input values.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/9: Minima and maxima are also called extrema.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/10: We can find local extrema from a graph. See {{link:0}} and {{link:1}}.
source_block_templates.fs-id1165135481952/item/11: The highest and lowest points on a graph indicate the maxima and minima. See {{link:0}}.
